claim: Caspase-8 is a key player in extrinsic apoptosis.
source: Caspase-8 is a key player in extrinsic apoptosis and its activity is often downregulated in cancer.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the role of Caspase-8 in apoptotic pathways.

claim: Caspase-8 activity is often downregulated in cancer.
source: Caspase-8 is a key player in extrinsic apoptosis and its activity is often downregulated in cancer.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and literature.

claim: Human Caspase-8 expression is retained in some tumors, including glioblastoma (GBM).
source: However, human Caspase-8 expression is retained in some tumors, including glioblastoma (GBM), suggesting that it may support cancer growth in these contexts.
evidence: This is stated as an observation that motivates the study.

claim: GBM is the most aggressive of the gliomas.
source: GBM, the most aggressive of the gliomas, is characterized by extensive angiogenesis and by an inflammatory microenvironment that support its development and resistance to therapies.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about GBM.

claim: GBM is characterized by extensive angiogenesis.
source: GBM, the most aggressive of the gliomas, is characterized by extensive angiogenesis and by an inflammatory microenvironment that support its development and resistance to therapies.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about GBM characteristics.

claim: GBM is characterized by an inflammatory microenvironment that supports its development and resistance to therapies.
source: GBM, the most aggressive of the gliomas, is characterized by extensive angiogenesis and by an inflammatory microenvironment that support its development and resistance to therapies.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about GBM characteristics.

claim: Caspase-8 sustains neoplastic transformation in vitro in human GBM cell lines.
source: We have recently shown that Caspase-8 sustains neoplastic transformation in vitro in human GBM cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by a prior publication by the authors (Fianco et al., 2016).

claim: Caspase-8, through activation of NF-kB, enhances the expression and secretion of VEGF, IL-6, IL-8, IL-1beta and MCP-1.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Caspase-8, through activation of NF-kB, enhances the expression and secretion of VEGF, IL-6, IL-8, IL-1beta and MCP-1, leading to neovascularization and increased resistance to Temozolomide.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Caspase-8-mediated enhancement of VEGF, IL-6, IL-8, IL-1beta and MCP-1 leads to neovascularization.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Caspase-8, through activation of NF-kB, enhances the expression and secretion of VEGF, IL-6, IL-8, IL-1beta and MCP-1, leading to neovascularization and increased resistance to Temozolomide.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from matrigel plug assays and tumor xenografts.

claim: Caspase-8-mediated enhancement of VEGF, IL-6, IL-8, IL-1beta and MCP-1 leads to increased resistance to Temozolomide.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Caspase-8, through activation of NF-kB, enhances the expression and secretion of VEGF, IL-6, IL-8, IL-1beta and MCP-1, leading to neovascularization and increased resistance to Temozolomide.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cell viability assays with TMZ treatment.

claim: High Caspase-8 expression levels correlate with a worse prognosis in high-grade human gliomas.
source: Importantly, the bioinformatics analysis of microarray gene expression data derived from a set of high-grade human gliomas, shows that high Caspase-8 expression levels correlate with a worse prognosis.
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis of patient data from microarray gene expression studies.

claim: Caspase-8 is a central player in the apoptotic cascade triggered by death receptors stimulation.
source: Caspase-8 is a central player in the apoptotic cascade triggered by death receptors stimulation (Juo et al., 1998); consistently, its expression (Pingoud-Meier et al., 2003) or its apoptotic activity (Cursi et al., 2006; Safa et al., 2008) are often reduced in cancer.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Juo et al., 1998.

claim: Caspase-8 expression is often reduced in cancer.
source: Caspase-8 is a central player in the apoptotic cascade triggered by death receptors stimulation (Juo et al., 1998); consistently, its expression (Pingoud-Meier et al., 2003) or its apoptotic activity (Cursi et al., 2006; Safa et al., 2008) are often reduced in cancer.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pingoud-Meier et al., 2003.

claim: Caspase-8 apoptotic activity is often reduced in cancer.
source: Caspase-8 is a central player in the apoptotic cascade triggered by death receptors stimulation (Juo et al., 1998); consistently, its expression (Pingoud-Meier et al., 2003) or its apoptotic activity (Cursi et al., 2006; Safa et al., 2008) are often reduced in cancer.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cursi et al., 2006 and Safa et al., 2008.

claim: Caspase-8 is retained in many tumors.
source: The observation that Caspase-8 is retained in many tumors (reviewed in [Stupack, 2013]) suggests a dual role for Caspase-8 in cancer.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Stupack, 2013.

claim: Caspase-8 has a dual role in cancer.
source: The observation that Caspase-8 is retained in many tumors (reviewed in [Stupack, 2013]) suggests a dual role for Caspase-8 in cancer.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Caspase-8 is retained in many tumors despite its pro-apoptotic function.

claim: Caspase-8 has several non-canonical functions that are independent of its enzymatic activity and of apoptosis.
source: The identification of several non-canonical functions of Caspase-8 that are independent of its enzymatic activity and of apoptosis, supports this idea.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Caspase-8 modulates cell adhesion and migration.
source: Indeed, Caspase-8 modulates cell adhesion and migration, suggesting that in cancer cells Caspase-8 may be rewired from apoptosis to alternative pathways that sustain tumor growth (reviewed in [Graf et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Graf et al., 2014.

claim: In cancer cells, Caspase-8 may be rewired from apoptosis to alternative pathways that sustain tumor growth.
source: Indeed, Caspase-8 modulates cell adhesion and migration, suggesting that in cancer cells Caspase-8 may be rewired from apoptosis to alternative pathways that sustain tumor growth (reviewed in [Graf et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the observation of non-canonical functions and cited review.

claim: Caspase-8 promotes the proliferation and neoplastic transformation of glioblastoma (GBM) cell lines.
source: We recently demonstrated that Caspase-8 promotes the proliferation and neoplastic transformation of glioblastoma (GBM) cell lines (Fianco et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' prior work (Fianco et al., 2016).

claim: Large-scale gene expression approaches have demonstrated Caspase-8 upregulation in GBM compared to normal tissue.
source: Interestingly, large-scale gene expression approaches have demonstrated Caspase-8 upregulation in GBM compared to normal tissue; in particular, the mesenchymal subtype of GBMs is characterized by high Caspase-8 expression (Verhaak et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Verhaak et al., 2010.

claim: The mesenchymal subtype of GBMs is characterized by high Caspase-8 expression.
source: Interestingly, large-scale gene expression approaches have demonstrated Caspase-8 upregulation in GBM compared to normal tissue; in particular, the mesenchymal subtype of GBMs is characterized by high Caspase-8 expression (Verhaak et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Verhaak et al., 2010.

claim: The fatal nature of GBM is strongly associated with its extensive angiogenesis.
source: The fatal nature of GBM is strongly associated with its extensive angiogenesis (Kargiotis et al., 2006), and with its capacity to infiltrate throughout the brain tissue and to resist to chemotherapy (Dunn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kargiotis et al., 2006.

claim: The fatal nature of GBM is strongly associated with its capacity to infiltrate throughout the brain tissue.
source: The fatal nature of GBM is strongly associated with its extensive angiogenesis (Kargiotis et al., 2006), and with its capacity to infiltrate throughout the brain tissue and to resist to chemotherapy (Dunn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dunn et al., 2012.

claim: The fatal nature of GBM is strongly associated with its capacity to resist chemotherapy.
source: The fatal nature of GBM is strongly associated with its extensive angiogenesis (Kargiotis et al., 2006), and with its capacity to infiltrate throughout the brain tissue and to resist to chemotherapy (Dunn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dunn et al., 2012.

claim: Tumor neoangiogenesis is strongly supported by an inflammatory microenvironment.
source: Tumor neoangiogenesis is strongly supported by an inflammatory microenvironment that also promotes the proliferation of tumor cells and the survival of malignant cells and alters responses to chemotherapeutic agents (Mantovani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mantovani et al., 2008.

claim: An inflammatory microenvironment promotes the proliferation of tumor cells.
source: Tumor neoangiogenesis is strongly supported by an inflammatory microenvironment that also promotes the proliferation of tumor cells and the survival of malignant cells and alters responses to chemotherapeutic agents (Mantovani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mantovani et al., 2008.

claim: An inflammatory microenvironment promotes the survival of malignant cells.
source: Tumor neoangiogenesis is strongly supported by an inflammatory microenvironment that also promotes the proliferation of tumor cells and the survival of malignant cells and alters responses to chemotherapeutic agents (Mantovani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mantovani et al., 2008.

claim: An inflammatory microenvironment alters responses to chemotherapeutic agents.
source: Tumor neoangiogenesis is strongly supported by an inflammatory microenvironment that also promotes the proliferation of tumor cells and the survival of malignant cells and alters responses to chemotherapeutic agents (Mantovani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mantovani et al., 2008.

claim: In vitro and in vivo studies have identified high levels of IL-8, IL-6 and IL-1beta in the conditioned media of several GBM cell lines and in microenvironment of clinical samples.
source: Consistently, in vitro and in vivo studies have identified high levels of IL-8, IL-6 and IL-1beta in the conditioned media (CM) of several GBM cell lines and in microenvironment of clinical samples (reviewed in Yeung et al., [2013]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Yeung et al., 2013.

claim: High levels of IL-8, IL-6 and IL-1beta in GBM often depend on overactive EGFR signalling.
source: This often depends on overactive EGFR signalling, which stimulates NF-kB, AP-1 and cEBP transcription factors, thereby promoting the expression of IL-8 and IL-6 (Bonavia et al., 2012; Inda et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bonavia et al., 2012 and Inda et al., 2010.

claim: Overactive EGFR signalling stimulates NF-kB, AP-1 and cEBP transcription factors.
source: This often depends on overactive EGFR signalling, which stimulates NF-kB, AP-1 and cEBP transcription factors, thereby promoting the expression of IL-8 and IL-6 (Bonavia et al., 2012; Inda et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bonavia et al., 2012 and Inda et al., 2010.

claim: EGFR signalling promotes the expression of IL-8 and IL-6 through NF-kB, AP-1 and cEBP transcription factors.
source: This often depends on overactive EGFR signalling, which stimulates NF-kB, AP-1 and cEBP transcription factors, thereby promoting the expression of IL-8 and IL-6 (Bonavia et al., 2012; Inda et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bonavia et al., 2012 and Inda et al., 2010.

claim: Caspase-8 is an activator of NF-kB in B cells downstream of antigen receptors.
source: The work of several laboratories has identified Caspase-8 as an activator of NF-kB in B cells downstream of antigen receptors (Su et al., 2005) and Toll-like receptors (Lemmers et al., 2007), as well as in T cells (Bidère et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Su et al., 2005.

claim: Caspase-8 is an activator of NF-kB in B cells downstream of Toll-like receptors.
source: The work of several laboratories has identified Caspase-8 as an activator of NF-kB in B cells downstream of antigen receptors (Su et al., 2005) and Toll-like receptors (Lemmers et al., 2007), as well as in T cells (Bidère et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lemmers et al., 2007.

claim: Caspase-8 is an activator of NF-kB in T cells.
source: The work of several laboratories has identified Caspase-8 as an activator of NF-kB in B cells downstream of antigen receptors (Su et al., 2005) and Toll-like receptors (Lemmers et al., 2007), as well as in T cells (Bidère et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bidère et al., 2006.

claim: NF-kB plays a pivotal role in modulating cytokine production.
source: These observations, along with the pivotal role of NF-kB in modulating cytokine production, in shaping tumor microenvironment and in promoting angiogenesis and GBM progression (reviewed in Karin et al. [2002], Dunn et al. [2012], Yeung et al. [2013] and Nogueira et al. [2011]), prompted us to investigate whether high Caspase-8 expression in GBM promotes these functions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews by Karin et al. 2002, Dunn et al. 2012, Yeung et al. 2013 and Nogueira et al. 2011.

claim: NF-kB plays a pivotal role in shaping tumor microenvironment.
source: These observations, along with the pivotal role of NF-kB in modulating cytokine production, in shaping tumor microenvironment and in promoting angiogenesis and GBM progression (reviewed in Karin et al. [2002], Dunn et al. [2012], Yeung et al. [2013] and Nogueira et al. [2011]), prompted us to investigate whether high Caspase-8 expression in GBM promotes these functions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews by Karin et al. 2002, Dunn et al. 2012, Yeung et al. 2013 and Nogueira et al. 2011.

claim: NF-kB plays a pivotal role in promoting angiogenesis.
source: These observations, along with the pivotal role of NF-kB in modulating cytokine production, in shaping tumor microenvironment and in promoting angiogenesis and GBM progression (reviewed in Karin et al. [2002], Dunn et al. [2012], Yeung et al. [2013] and Nogueira et al. [2011]), prompted us to investigate whether high Caspase-8 expression in GBM promotes these functions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews by Karin et al. 2002, Dunn et al. 2012, Yeung et al. 2013 and Nogueira et al. 2011.

claim: NF-kB plays a pivotal role in promoting GBM progression.
source: These observations, along with the pivotal role of NF-kB in modulating cytokine production, in shaping tumor microenvironment and in promoting angiogenesis and GBM progression (reviewed in Karin et al. [2002], Dunn et al. [2012], Yeung et al. [2013] and Nogueira et al. [2011]), prompted us to investigate whether high Caspase-8 expression in GBM promotes these functions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews by Karin et al. 2002, Dunn et al. 2012, Yeung et al. 2013 and Nogueira et al. 2011.

claim: Matrigel plugs containing CM from U87CTR induced a strong angiogenic response similar to that detected in the positive control where VEGF has been added to the media.
source: Matrigel plugs containing CM from U87CTR induced a strong angiogenic response as evidenced by macroscopic analysis and haemoglobin content, similar to that detected in the positive control where VEGF has been added to the media.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Matrigel plugs containing CM from U87 shC8 displayed a significant reduction of both angiogenesis in vivo and the haemoglobin content.
source: Importantly, matrigel plugs containing CM from U87 shC8 displayed a significant reduction of both angiogenesis in vivo and the haemoglobin content (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: CM from U87shC8 cells was 2.5-fold less potent in triggering the proliferation of Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells (HUVECs) compared to CM from U87CTR cells.
source: In agreement with this finding, CM from U87shC8 cells was 2.5-fold less potent in triggering the proliferation of Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells (HUVECs) compared to CM from U87CTR cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: When exposed to CM from U87CTR cells, HUVECs formed tube-like structures resembling a capillary plexus.
source: Moreover, when exposed to CM from U87CTR cells, HUVECs formed tube-like structures resembling a capillary plexus; conversely, partially organized and rounded endothelial cells were observed after the addition of CM from U87shC8 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Partially organized and rounded endothelial cells were observed after the addition of CM from U87shC8 cells.
source: Moreover, when exposed to CM from U87CTR cells, HUVECs formed tube-like structures resembling a capillary plexus; conversely, partially organized and rounded endothelial cells were observed after the addition of CM from U87shC8 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: After three weeks, U87 cells formed tumors of an average volume of ~1,254 mm3 in all injected mice.
source: As reported in Figure 1C, after three weeks, U87 cells formed tumors of an average volume of ~1,254 mm3 in all injected mice, whereas U87shC8 cells exhibited a drastically reduced capacity to form tumors (mean tumor volume: ~148 mm3), which were detected in only 29% of injected mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: U87shC8 cells exhibited a drastically reduced capacity to form tumors (mean tumor volume: ~148 mm3), which were detected in only 29% of injected mice after three weeks.
source: As reported in Figure 1C, after three weeks, U87 cells formed tumors of an average volume of ~1,254 mm3 in all injected mice, whereas U87shC8 cells exhibited a drastically reduced capacity to form tumors (mean tumor volume: ~148 mm3), which were detected in only 29% of injected mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: After 6 weeks, the mean tumor volume generated by U87sh8 cells was ~344 mm3 and tumors were identified in 67% of injected mice.
source: After 6 weeks, the mean tumor volume generated by U87sh8 cells was ~344 mm3 and tumors were identified in 67% of injected mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was a significant difference in vascularization between CTR and shC8 tumors.
source: Figure 1D shows that there was a significant difference in vascularization between CTR and shC8 tumors; the mean number of vessels per mm2 field was 20.52 (±0.62) for CTR and 1.21 (±0.41) for shC8 (p=0.001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The mean number of vessels per mm2 field was 20.52 (±0.62) for CTR and 1.21 (±0.41) for shC8 (p=0.001).
source: Figure 1D shows that there was a significant difference in vascularization between CTR and shC8 tumors; the mean number of vessels per mm2 field was 20.52 (±0.62) for CTR and 1.21 (±0.41) for shC8 (p=0.001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Caspase-8 expression in GBM is required for tumor growth.
source: Overall, these data suggest that Caspase-8 expression in GBM is required for tumor growth, maximal proliferation of GBM-associated endothelial cells and angiogenesis, probably through the production of secreted factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced tumor growth in Caspase-8 silenced cells.

claim: Caspase-8 expression in GBM is required for maximal proliferation of GBM-associated endothelial cells.
source: Overall, these data suggest that Caspase-8 expression in GBM is required for tumor growth, maximal proliferation of GBM-associated endothelial cells and angiogenesis, probably through the production of secreted factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced HUVEC proliferation with CM from Caspase-8 silenced cells.

claim: Caspase-8 expression in GBM is required for angiogenesis, probably through the production of secreted factors.
source: Overall, these data suggest that Caspase-8 expression in GBM is required for tumor growth, maximal proliferation of GBM-associated endothelial cells and angiogenesis, probably through the production of secreted factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced angiogenesis with CM from Caspase-8 silenced cells.

claim: High levels of IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, MCP-1, VEGF-A and TNFalpha were present in the CM of U87CTR.
source: High levels of IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, MCP-1, VEGF-A and TNFalpha were present in the CM of U87CTR, as is consistent with previous reports (Albulescu et al., 2013), and the genetic inhibition of Caspase-8 caused a strong decrease in the levels of these cytokines (except TNF alpha) in the CM (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and citation to Albulescu et al., 2013.

claim: The genetic inhibition of Caspase-8 caused a strong decrease in the levels of IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, MCP-1, and VEGF-A (except TNF alpha) in the CM.
source: High levels of IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, MCP-1, VEGF-A and TNFalpha were present in the CM of U87CTR, as is consistent with previous reports (Albulescu et al., 2013), and the genetic inhibition of Caspase-8 caused a strong decrease in the levels of these cytokines (except TNF alpha) in the CM (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A dramatic reduction of IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, MCP-1, and VEGF-A mRNAs was observed upon Caspase-8 downregulation.
source: Accordingly, we observed a dramatic reduction of the respective mRNAs upon Caspase-8 downregulation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Similar results were obtained in U87 cells where Caspase-8 expression was inhibited using a different interfering sequence.
source: We obtained similar results in U87 cells where Caspase-8 expression was inhibited using a different interfering sequence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as well as in U251, another GBM cell line (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Similar results were obtained in U251, another GBM cell line.
source: We obtained similar results in U87 cells where Caspase-8 expression was inhibited using a different interfering sequence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as well as in U251, another GBM cell line (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Caspase-8 expression profile positively correlated with those of IL-6, IL-8, IL1β and MCP-1 in 174 human GBM patients.
source: Interestingly, the Caspase-8 expression profile positively correlated with those of IL-6, IL-8, IL1β and MCP-1 (Figure 2C and Figure 2—source data 4), ranging from 0.25 when comparing the Caspase-8 and IL-6 GBM expression profiles, to 0.53 for Caspase-8 and MCP-1.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis of RNA-seq data from TCGA shown in Figure 2C.

claim: All correlations between Caspase-8 and IL-6, IL-8, IL1β and MCP-1 were statistically significant (P-value < 0.0008 for each comparison).
source: All of these correlations were statistically significant (P-value < 0.0008 for each comparison), whereas there was no significant relationship between the Caspase-8 and VEGF expression profiles (Pearson correlation coefficient 0.09, p-value 0.22).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the correlation data.

claim: There was no significant relationship between the Caspase-8 and VEGF expression profiles (Pearson correlation coefficient 0.09, p-value 0.22).
source: All of these correlations were statistically significant (P-value < 0.0008 for each comparison), whereas there was no significant relationship between the Caspase-8 and VEGF expression profiles (Pearson correlation coefficient 0.09, p-value 0.22).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the correlation data.

claim: These results identified a novel role of Caspase-8 in promoting neoangiogenesis.
source: Overall these results identified a novel role of Caspase-8 in promoting neoangiogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing Caspase-8's role in cytokine production and angiogenesis.

claim: Caspase-8 null mice showed defects in the angiogenesis programme during development.
source: This is in agreement with previous studies on Caspase-8 null mice, which showed defects in the angiogenesis programme during development (Scharner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Scharner et al., 2009.

claim: The overexpression of a dominant negative mutant of IKBalpha (IKBaphaS32A/S36A, named IKBapha SR) that inhibits NF-kB signalling severely decreased the expression of IL-6, IL-8, IL1β, MCP-1 and VEGF-A mRNAs in U87 cells.
source: Consistently, the overexpression of a dominant negative mutant of IKBalpha (IKBaphaS32A/S36A, named IKBapha SR) that inhibits NF-kB signalling severely decreased the expression of IL-6, IL-8, IL1β, MCP-1 and VEGF-A mRNAs in U87 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Silencing of Caspase-8 in U87 cells did not reduce the amount of NF-kB but strongly decreased its nuclear localization.
source: Silencing of Caspase-8 in U87 cells did not reduce the amount of NF-kB but strongly decreased its nuclear localization (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Similar results were also obtained in U251 GBM cells.
source: Similar results were also obtained in U251 GBM cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Preliminary immunohistochemistry analysis in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissues suggests a different distribution of NF-kB in CTR (nuclear and cytoplasmic) and in shC8 (mainly cytoplasmic) tumors.
source: Preliminary immunohistochemistry analysis in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissues suggests a different distribution of NF-kB in CTR (nuclear and cytoplasmic) and in shC8 (mainly cytoplasmic) tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A significant reduction of VEGF and IL-8 mRNA levels was detected in shC8-derived tumor samples.
source: Consistently, we could detect a significant reduction of VEGF and IL-8 mRNA levels in shC8-derived tumor samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: These results provide the first evidence that Caspase-8 promotes NF-kB activity in GBM in vitro and in vivo.
source: Our results provide the first evidence that Caspase-8 promotes NF-kB activity in GBM in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing Caspase-8's effect on NF-kB nuclear localization.

claim: Cancer-associated missense mutations of Caspase-8 resulting in stronger activation of NF-kB have been identified recently in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
source: Interestingly, cancer-associated missense mutations of Caspase-8 resulting in stronger activation of NF-kB have been identified recently in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (Ando et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ando et al., 2013.

claim: The down-regulation of Caspase-8 expression significantly sensitized U87 cells to the cytotoxic effects of TMZ.
source: As shown in Figure 4A and in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, the down-regulation of Caspase-8 expression significantly sensitized U87 cells to the cytotoxic effects of TMZ.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of the dominant negative mutant of IKBalpha, IKBaphaSR, had a similar effect to Caspase-8 silencing in sensitizing cells to TMZ.
source: Interestingly, the expression of the dominant negative mutant of IKBalpha, IKBaphaSR, had a similar effect (Figure 4B), suggesting that Caspase-8 exerts its function via NF-kB signalling, possibly through secreted cytokines.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Caspase-8 exerts its function via NF-kB signalling, possibly through secreted cytokines.
source: Interestingly, the expression of the dominant negative mutant of IKBalpha, IKBaphaSR, had a similar effect (Figure 4B), suggesting that Caspase-8 exerts its function via NF-kB signalling, possibly through secreted cytokines.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar effects of Caspase-8 silencing and IKBalpha SR expression on TMZ sensitivity.

claim: CM of control cells that endogenously express Caspase-8 was sufficient to restore resistance to TMZ in cells silenced for Caspase-8.
source: Indeed, as shown in Figure 4C, CM of control cells that endogenously express Caspase-8 was sufficient to restore resistance to TMZ in cells silenced for Caspase-8.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CM from IKBalphaSR-expressing cells, like that from Caspase-8-deficient cells, lost the protective capability against TMZ.
source: Importantly, CM from IKBalphaSR-expressing cells, like that from Caspase-8-deficient cells, lost such a protective capability (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Caspase-8 expression in GBM cells triggers resistance to TMZ via an autocrine loop.
source: These results support the conclusion that Caspase-8 expression in GBM cells triggers resistance to TMZ via an autocrine loop and suggest that the level of Caspase-8 expression may correlate with prognosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that CM from control cells can restore TMZ resistance.

claim: The level of Caspase-8 expression may correlate with prognosis.
source: These results support the conclusion that Caspase-8 expression in GBM cells triggers resistance to TMZ via an autocrine loop and suggest that the level of Caspase-8 expression may correlate with prognosis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: Patients that have higher Caspase-8 expression levels have a lower survival chance than those with lower expression (Chi-squared 10.5 on 1 degree of freedom, p-value 0.00117).
source: Analysis of the survival curves shows that patients that have higher Caspase-8 expression levels have a lower survival chance than those with lower expression (Chi-squared 10.5 on 1 degree of freedom, p-value 0.00117), supporting our hypothesis (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis of 77 high-grade glioma patients shown in Figure 4E.

claim: For patients classified as proneural, those having high Caspase-8 expression show significantly lower survival probability (Chi-squared 7.2 on 1 degree of freedom, p-value 0.00732).
source: For patients classified as proneural, those having high Caspase-8 expression show significantly lower survival probability (Chi-squared 7.2 on 1 degree of freedom, p-value 0.00732), while no difference was observed for the mesenchymal and proliferative subtypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis of proneural subtype patients shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: No difference in survival was observed for the mesenchymal and proliferative subtypes based on Caspase-8 expression.
source: For patients classified as proneural, those having high Caspase-8 expression show significantly lower survival probability (Chi-squared 7.2 on 1 degree of freedom, p-value 0.00732), while no difference was observed for the mesenchymal and proliferative subtypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The classical role of Caspase-8 in apoptosis may account for the correlation between loss of Caspase-8 expression and unfavourable prognosis in medulloblastoma.
source: The classical role of Caspase-8 in apoptosis may account for the correlation between loss of Caspase-8 expression and unfavourable prognosis in medulloblastoma (Pingoud-Meier et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pingoud-Meier et al., 2003.

claim: Tumors that are strongly dependent on NFkB activity and cytokine production, such as GBM, may have a selective advantage in retaining Caspase-8 expression.
source: Conversely, tumors that are strongly dependent on NFkB activity and cytokine production, such as GBM, may have a selective advantage in retaining Caspase-8 expression.
